strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP evaluation problem: how collaborative workflows affect interactive qualitative coding. Studying three different system families and two contrasting corpora provides useful descriptive evidence.

The evaluation distinguishes consistency, cohesiveness, distinctiveness, and assignment correctness. The manual assessment of 2,400 document–theme pairs, with two annotators and adjudication, provides valuable evidence beyond embedding metrics; annotator agreement is reported transparently.
The manuscript documents system operations, initialization choices, prompt templates, and final theme lists, and links code and experimental data. These are useful provisions for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The design does not isolate collaboration modality. Section 4 compares individual coders with three-person synchronous teams, without consolidating the independent codebooks into an asynchronous team outcome. Team size and deliberation therefore change together. Repeat participants always complete asynchronous work first, introducing possible learning effects, while participant allocation and time budgets are insufficiently documented. The results support a narrower comparison of these configurations than the claimed effects of synchronous versus asynchronous collaboration.

The statistical evidence is insufficiently justified. Each system–dataset combination has only two synchronous codebooks and three asynchronous codebooks, yet Tables 1–2 report numerous significant differences using unpaired t-tests without identifying the observations or degrees of freedom. Themes and document similarities within a codebook are dependent, and some participants recur. For example, Climate relational cohesion of 0.44 versus 0.43 is marked significant despite standard deviations of 0.10 and 0.09. Analysis must respect codebook and participant dependence, report uncertainty, and address multiple comparisons.

The proposed quality framework needs stronger validation. Maximum-overlap matching permits many-to-one alignments and is sensitive to theme granularity; Table 17 shows substantial differences in theme counts. High SBERT similarity does not necessarily establish agreement on interpretive themes, especially opposing positions sharing vocabulary. Selecting centroid-near documents for the top-quartile analysis further favors embedding coherence. Sensitivity analyses and expert assessment of thematic usefulness are needed before interpreting these proxies as better qualitative analysis.

Correctness is inadequately specified. Section 5.3 describes checking proposed document–theme assignments, while Figure 4 labels the outcome F1 without defining precision, recall, missed assignments, or aggregation. As described, the audit supports assignment precision rather than a complete classification F1 evaluation. The treatment of unmapped documents is also unclear, although Table 4 reports invalid LLM labels for up to 16.1% of a corpus. Sampling weights, coverage, annotation instructions, and uncertainty are needed to interpret system comparisons.

Important procedural ambiguities limit reproducibility. Tables 15–16 list the same Climate theme sets for corresponding relational and LLM sessions, but the manuscript does not explain whether these codebooks were reused or independently elicited. This matters for interpreting the reported experiments and cross-system evidence. The interview study also omits its sample size and analysis procedure, leaving broad experiential conclusions supported mainly by a few quotations.

Several conclusions exceed the evidence. Two corpora differing simultaneously in topic, platform, size, length, and repetition cannot establish independent effects of particular dataset characteristics. Discussion depth and cognitive load are proposed explanations rather than measured outcomes. Likewise, broad conclusions about LLM inefficiency and unreliability derive from one 3B model and prompting configuration. The useful exploratory contribution could support a revised submission, but the design interpretation, statistical analysis, and correctness reporting require important revisions before a sound Findings recommendation.
